title: The US has no good options in Iran, and an AI kill switch won't stop the models
dek: Iran's terrain makes any ground war a non-starter, and the war of attrition at Hormuz is burning through the US military's global deployment margin; the real problem in AI regulation isn't giving DHS a kill switch, it's that nobody wants to control compute, the raw material.
why: The first half is a hardcore walkthrough of US military logistics and Iranian terrain; the second half, on AI regulation and Ukrainian civil-military relations, drops off noticeably in density, so you can listen to just the first half.
who: Founders, investors and engineers tracking Middle East military logistics, US force readiness and the direction of AI regulation policy, especially anyone who wants to understand how the war of attrition at Hormuz burns through the US military's global deployment margin.
skip: After 38:50, the discussion of daylight saving time and the AI kill switch is lower density and can be skipped.

points.h: A supply ship winning a presidential award means the fleet is already at its limit
points.body: Two carrier strike groups have been in the Arabian Sea for a long time and cannot enter ports like Bahrain to replenish, so the Navy can only send oilers from Europe, Crete or the Pacific to transfer fuel at sea to replenishment oilers in the Arabian Sea, which then distribute it to ships and carrier air wings. This "daisy chain" has to stretch thousands of miles. The crew and military detachment of one supply ship received a Presidential Unit Citation for nearly a year of 24-7 support, which is itself a signal that the fleet has been pushed to its limit. A normal surface ship deployment is about seven months; many are now at eleven months, close to a year.

points.h: Pulling ships forward early burns through future readiness reserves
points.body: The normal cycle for a surface ship is three years: a seven-month deployment, then maintenance, training, local operations and workups, then another deployment about two to two and a half years after maintenance ends. Now the Navy has to pull ships out of the normal cycle early to replace ships that have been out for nearly a year. The problem is that interrupting training and maintenance cycles early means ships break down once they get to sea and very likely have to return to port early. The end result is that reserve capacity gets burned up and ships are forced off deployment because they are broken. The McCain and Fitzgerald collisions in the late 2010s were the consequence of overuse and insufficient maintenance.

points.h: Iran's terrain leaves almost no entry point for a ground war
points.body: Inside the Pentagon there are discussions, pushed by Marines and military commanders, about seizing islands including Karg Island and starting to take ground. But Iran is hard to attack from every direction: the southwest is the marshes where the Marsh Arabs live, which made Saddam's mechanized forces hard to move through; the north is the Alborz mountains, high and difficult; the east is the Baluch desert, basically salt flats. Every province has IRGC, Quds Force and Basij recruitment stations, so any attack will bring local militias up. And the US no longer has a Navy or Coast Guard presence in the Persian Gulf, many bases will not be rebuilt, and ground forces would be operating essentially in isolation.

points.h: Fuel can be transferred at sea, food cannot
points.body: The Navy designed a tanker-to-oiler-to-ship transfer model for fuel, but there is no similar scheme for food. Cargo ships carrying food have to come from very far away, the military still requires food to come from the US, there is almost no opportunity to buy locally, and supply officers can no longer go ashore to buy food the way they used to. Feeding two carrier strike groups is itself a huge undertaking. If they are out for a year, the good food runs out first and only frozen food is left, and there are no MREs on board. They have to redesign a model for how to feed at sea in an environment where the supply line is contested.

points.h: Global bases are not an empire, they are the logistics skeleton
points.body: The point of the global force posture is to serve as the skeleton of logistics hubs and logistics models that let forces flow into a region to protect critical national interests. The US has already been shrinking that skeleton in Europe and the Middle East, and now it is under attack, which means losing the skeleton for doing the next big thing in the region. The problem with this administration is that it first pursued a "denial" strategy, doing more in this hemisphere and less elsewhere, stripping away the capabilities needed to sustain combat power, and then used combat power in various places anyway. A father in the military once said that behind every infantryman there are twenty support personnel responsible for paying, clothing, feeding and maintaining equipment, and those are exactly what has been removed from Europe and the Middle East.

points.h: If it can reverse itself on Saudi Arabia at any moment, why should Iran negotiate
points.body: The US announced it would allow Saudi Arabia to develop nuclear energy, and the two sides signed documents, but then the White House press secretary said the president was changing it, and what he posts on Truth Social is government policy. In other words, an agreement with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia can be changed on a whim, without consulting the Saudis. Iran sees this: if even an ally's agreement can be reversed in an instant, what do the people inside Iran who want to negotiate use to persuade the hardliners who do not want to do deals with the US? This directly weakens the incentive to negotiate. At the same time, the Houthi blockade of Bab al-Mandeb cuts off Saudi Arabia's alternative route for exporting oil via the Red Sea, and the pressure will feed through to oil markets and push the price per barrel higher.

points.h: If you are going to strike, make it an air campaign like the one before the Iraq war, otherwise don't
points.body: The optimistic scenario is: this time hit the right targets, and stop hitting the kind of random strike plans "written by the world's worst staff officers who were bored in the desert." To really apply pressure, you have to keep hitting every target that lets Iran control or disrupt the strait, like the air campaign before the invasion of Iraq, which requires taking on a lot of risk and a huge amount of capability, and you cannot stop. The problem is that the US military has been unwilling to do this, because precision weapons are limited in number, hitting Shahed launchers along the coastline means the terrain is too rugged, you have to use laser-guided bombs, aircraft have to get close to the target, and you need suppression of enemy air defenses and F-22 escorts, which significantly increases exposure. At the same time you have to escort commercial shipping, because there will always be leakers.

points.h: From high-value targets to high-payoff targets, it still comes down to people
points.body: Turning a high-value target list into a high-payoff target list is staff work, requiring people to sit down and do "work that doesn't fudge," judging whether a target is really important to the enemy. This step still depends on human decision-making and cannot be replaced by Palantir or similar companies. The US military is not doing this now, it is just striking what is already on the list. Another thing that must be done is escorting: to take away Iran's leverage, you have to keep hitting targets along the coastline that threaten shipping, while sending ships to defend at sea against leakers, missiles and drones. This is a huge exercise in trust, and many companies currently do not believe the US can do it, so it has to be proven through action.
